title: The ten words, part one (Exodus 20:1–11)
hookLine: no other gods, no idols, God's name in honor, the sabbath kept

lines: ON WALLS, IN STONE, IN COURT.
cards: They hang on courthouse walls and in Sunday school classrooms. They've been carved in stone, stitched on samplers, fought over in lawsuits, and turned into a movie with a parting sea. Can you name all ten?
And which one comes first? No other gods is a fair guess. But that isn't quite the first thing the voice on the mountain says.
Before a single command, there's a sentence about who is speaking, and what he has already done. Today, the first half of the ten words: the ones about God.

teach.h: A RESCUE COMES BEFORE ANY RULE.
teach.b: Here is how the voice begins, in the King James Bible: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." A rescue comes before any rule.
You're already free, the text says, and here is how free people live. Then: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." No carved image to bow down to.
Don't take God's name in vain, which means more than swearing: don't use the name emptily, or to prop up a lie. And: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."
Six days of work and a seventh of rest, for you, your children, your servants, the stranger living with you, even your cattle. The reason given is creation: God rested on the seventh day.
In Hebrew, Exodus calls them aseret ha-devarim, the ten words. Decalogue is the Greek version: deka, ten, logos, word. And traditions count the ten differently.
In Jewish tradition, the opening sentence, I am the LORD thy God, is the first word.

teach.h: NO OTHER GODS, NO IMAGES, NO EMPTY NAME.
teach.b: Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, put no other gods and no images together, and split coveting into two at the end.

Orthodox Christians and Reformed and Anglican churches make the images a separate second commandment. Same text, different numbering, and nobody is leaving anything out. What all of them see is the order.
The first words point at God.

teach.h: THOU SHALT HAVE NO OTHER GODS BEFORE ME.
teach.b: Everything else follows from what you put first.

how: Christians learn the Ten Commandments in catechism classes and Sunday schools, and some churches read them aloud in worship; Catholic and Lutheran catechisms number them one way, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican churches another.

games.q: you're at the foot of Sinai, waiting for the first command. what does the voice say first?
o: thou shalt have no other gods.
I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of Egypt.
games.why: before any rule, a reminder of rescue. in Jewish tradition that sentence is itself the first of the ten words.

practice: Think back over the last week: what got your first hour, what you checked before anything else, what you arrange everything else around. Name it honestly, without judging, then ask whether it's what you'd choose to put first.
If you pray, you can hear the opening line again, I am the LORD thy God; if you don't, simply hold the question.

wordCard.voice: Decalogue. Greek for the ten words, the Bible's own name for the commandments given at Sinai. The first ones are about God.

orig.note: Greek: deka, ten, and logos, word. It translates the Hebrew aseret ha-devarim, the ten words.
